paragraphs.title: The Lord Appears as an Avenging and Punishing God

easy.q: To whom is the burden at the beginning of Nahum addressed?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth.”
easy.q: How is God described in verse 2?

easy.explanation: Nahum 1:3 says, “the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm.”
easy.q: What accompanies the Lord’s way according to verse 3?

answers: He is slow to anger but does not clear the guilty
He is always angry and never patient
medium.explanation: The Lord is “slow to anger,” yet “will not at all acquit the wicked.”
medium.q: Which combination correctly describes the Lord in verses 2–3?

answers: He keeps judgment in store for His enemies
He forgets the actions of His enemies
He protects His enemies from judgment
medium.explanation: The phrase indicates that the Lord retains wrath for those who oppose Him.
medium.q: What does the phrase “he reserveth wrath for his enemies” mean?

answers: To emphasize His power and coming judgment
To show that He is hiding
medium.explanation: The whirlwind and storm picture the Lord’s powerful appearance in judgment.
medium.q: Why is the Lord’s way described with storm imagery?

answers: He is slow to anger, yet He will punish the guilty
He is powerless, yet He appears strong
He is absent, yet He is mentioned
challenge.explanation: The passage joins divine patience with certainty of judgment.
challenge.q: What tension appears in the description of the Lord in these verses?

answers: The overwhelming majesty of the Lord’s presence
challenge.explanation: The storm serves as a picture of the Lord’s power and authority.
challenge.q: What does the storm imagery communicate beyond the weather itself?

challenge.explanation: The Lord takes vengeance on His adversaries and reserves wrath for His enemies.
challenge.q: Who receives the Lord’s vengeance according to verse 2?

answers: It covers the sea with earth
easy.explanation: Nahum 1:4 says, “He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry.”
easy.q: What does the Lord’s rebuke do to the sea?

easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “The mountains quake at him.”
easy.q: What happens to the mountains before the Lord?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “the rocks are thrown down by him.”
easy.q: What happens to the rocks because of the Lord?

answers: The sea dries, the rivers wither, and the mountains quake
The sea rises, the rivers grow, and the mountains bloom
The sea becomes calm, the rivers fill, and the hills strengthen
medium.explanation: These events are described in Nahum 1:4–5.
medium.q: Which sequence best summarizes the Lord’s power over nature?

medium.explanation: The word describes fertile places drying up or losing their vitality.
medium.q: In context, what does “languisheth” mean in “Bashan languisheth, and Carmel”?

medium.explanation: Nahum 1:6 asks, “Who can stand before his indignation?”
medium.q: What question is asked about standing before the Lord’s indignation?

answers: To show the Lord’s authority over the whole created order
To identify one small geographical location
To suggest that nature is stronger than God
challenge.explanation: The variety of natural features broadens the picture of divine power.
challenge.q: Why are the sea, rivers, fertile lands, mountains, and hills all mentioned?

answers: If creation cannot withstand Him, no one can resist His anger
Creation is unrelated to the Lord’s anger
People are stronger than the natural world
challenge.explanation: The shaking mountains and melting hills illustrate the irresistible force of His indignation.
challenge.q: How does the trembling creation support the questions in verse 6?

answers: A sense of upheaval and destruction
A sense of rest and safety
A sense of growth and renewal
challenge.explanation: These forceful verbs portray creation collapsing before the Lord.
challenge.q: What effect is created by the verbs “quake,” “melt,” and “burned”?

paragraphs.title: The Lord Protects Those Who Trust in Him

easy.explanation: Nahum 1:7 calls the Lord “a strong hold in the day of trouble.”
easy.q: What is the Lord in the day of trouble?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “he knoweth them that trust in him.”
Nahum 1:8 says, “darkness shall pursue his enemies.”

answers: The Lord protects those who trust Him but destroys wickedness
The Lord punishes those who trust Him but protects evil
The Lord ignores both the faithful and the wicked
medium.explanation: The verses contrast the Lord’s goodness toward the faithful with judgment on evil.

answers: A place of protection and strength
medium.explanation: A strong hold is a secure refuge or fortified place.
medium.q: What does “a strong hold” mean in verse 7?

answers: A sweeping force that brings complete destruction
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures overwhelming judgment that makes an utter end.
medium.q: What does “an overrunning flood” suggest in verse 8?

answers: It shows that the Lord is good and protects those who trust Him
It cancels the earlier descriptions of His power
challenge.explanation: The verse shows that divine judgment does not contradict the Lord’s goodness toward His people.
challenge.q: How does verse 7 balance the descriptions of divine anger?

answers: The faithful are known and protected, while the enemies are pursued by darkness
Both groups receive exactly the same treatment
challenge.explanation: The passage presents protection for the trusting and judgment for the enemies.
challenge.q: What distinction is made between those who trust in the Lord and His enemies?

answers: The enemies’ coming judgment and ruin
challenge.explanation: Darkness represents the destruction and hopeless outcome awaiting the Lord’s enemies.
challenge.q: What does darkness symbolize in verse 8?

paragraphs.title: The Destruction of the Assyrian Enemies

answers: What do ye imagine against the LORD?
Where do ye worship the LORD?
Why do ye trust in the LORD?
easy.explanation: Nahum 1:9 begins with the question, “What do ye imagine against the LORD?”
easy.q: What does the Lord ask His enemies in verse 9?

easy.explanation: The enemies are described as tangled thorns, drunkards, and fully dry stubble.
easy.q: What are the enemies compared to in verse 10?

answers: One who imagined evil against the Lord
easy.explanation: Verse 11 speaks of one who came out of Nineveh and imagined evil against the Lord.
easy.q: What came out of Nineveh according to verse 11?

answers: Folden together as thorns, drunken as drunkards, and dry as stubble
Growing like trees and flowing like rivers
Ruling like kings and defending like soldiers
medium.explanation: These three images describe the enemies’ condition before their destruction.

answers: A person who gives evil advice
medium.explanation: The phrase identifies someone who plans or advises wickedness.
The Lord declares that He will “make an utter end.”
medium.q: What will the Lord do to the enemies according to verse 9?

answers: They suggest instability, weakness, and ease of destruction
They suggest wisdom and lasting strength
They show that the enemies are well protected
challenge.explanation: Drunkards are unstable and dry stubble is easily consumed, emphasizing the enemies’ weakness.
challenge.q: Why do the images of drunkards and dry stubble strengthen the description of destruction?

answers: It challenges the enemies’ ability to oppose God successfully
It asks them to improve their plans
challenge.explanation: The question implies that their plans against the Lord are futile.
challenge.q: What force does the question “What do ye imagine against the LORD?” have in the passage?

answers: They plan evil against the Lord, but their plan ends in destruction
They plan evil and succeed permanently
They make no plans at all
challenge.explanation: The wicked counsellor’s scheme cannot prevent the Lord from making an utter end.
challenge.q: How are the enemies’ plans related to their final outcome?

paragraphs.title: Breaking Assyria’s Yoke and Judging It

answers: They will be cut down and pass away
easy.explanation: Though they are many, they will be cut down when the Lord passes through.
easy.q: What will happen to Assyria even though its forces are many?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will break his yoke from off thee.”
easy.q: What will the Lord do to the yoke of Assyria?

easy.explanation: The Lord declares, “out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image.”
easy.q: What will the Lord do to the graven and molten images?

answers: Assyria is numerous but will be cut down, while Judah’s affliction will end
Assyria is weak while Judah disappears
Assyria and Judah remain in the same condition
medium.explanation: The verse contrasts Assyria’s destruction with the end of Judah’s affliction.
To burst bonds in sunder is to break the restraints into pieces.
medium.q: What does “burst thy bonds in sunder” mean?

answers: Because Assyria is vile in His sight
Because Assyria built a temple to the Lord
medium.explanation: The verse concludes, “I will make thy grave; for thou art vile.”
medium.q: Why does the Lord say He will make Assyria’s grave?

answers: The end of Assyrian oppression over Judah
The beginning of a new oppression
challenge.explanation: The yoke and bonds represent the burden of Assyrian domination, which the Lord removes.
challenge.q: What does breaking the yoke and bonds symbolize?

answers: Both show the rejection and removal of Assyria’s power
Both show the Lord protecting Assyria
challenge.explanation: The idols and Assyria’s authority are both declared subject to removal.
challenge.q: How are the destruction of the idols and the judgment of Assyria connected?

answers: Large numbers and apparent strength cannot prevent sudden destruction
The army will remain permanently strong
challenge.explanation: Even a numerous and seemingly secure force can be quickly destroyed by the Lord.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between “quiet, and likewise many” and “cut down” teach?
